subject: Cooking
title: Basil: The King of Herbs
description: A 60-second lesson on Basil: The King of Herbs.

hook.text: The word 'basil' comes from the Greek 'basilikon' meaning 'royal.' It was considered the king of herbs.

buildup.text: Sweet basil, Thai basil, holy basil, and lemon basil — over 60 varieties exist worldwide.

discovery.text: Basil's signature flavor comes from linalool and eugenol — compounds shared with lavender and cloves.

twist.text: Heat destroys basil's delicate oils in seconds. That's why Italian chefs add it last, torn — never chopped.

climax.text: Thai basil is the exception — its sturdy leaves survive high heat, making it perfect for stir-fries.

punchline.text: The king of herbs has one weakness: heat.

quiz.question: Why do Italian chefs add basil at the very end of cooking?
options: It needs to stay raw to be safe

details.summary: Basil's complex flavor comes from volatile oils including linalool, eugenol, and estragole that degrade rapidly when heated. Over 60 basil varieties range from sweet Italian to Thai to lemon basil. Adding it at the end of cooking preserves the delicate aromatic compounds that define its character.
details.whyItMatters: Basil is one of the most widely used fresh herbs worldwide. Knowing when and how to use it — fresh versus dried, early versus late — transforms dishes from flat to vibrant.
takeaways: Volatile oils break down within minutes of heating
Sweet basil dominates Italian cooking; Thai basil suits Asian dishes
Adding basil at the end preserves its aromatic complexity

faq.question: Why does basil turn black in the refrigerator?
faq.answer: Basil is tropical and suffers cold injury below 50°F. Cell membranes break down in the cold, causing enzymatic browning that turns leaves black. Store basil at room temperature in water like a bouquet, or wrap loosely and refrigerate only short-term above 50°F.

faq.question: What is the difference between sweet basil and Thai basil?
faq.answer: Sweet basil has a delicate, peppery flavor with anise notes that dissipate with heat. Thai basil has a stronger licorice flavor, sturdier leaves, and holds up to cooking much better. Thai basil is essential for curries and stir-fries; sweet basil is best raw.
